claims.text: High-entropy nanoalloys are relevant to high-temperature applications.
High configurational entropy creates kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion.
The kinetic barriers associated with high configurational entropy produce sluggish diffusion.
Sluggish diffusion suppresses diffusion-driven chemical clustering.
Inhibition of microstructural rearrangement governs the structural and chemical stability of the nanoalloy.
The tested initial material is a homogeneous, single-phase, equiatomic nanoalloy with nanostructured grains.
Skewing the elemental ratios away from equiatomic proportions lowers configurational entropy.
Grain boundaries mediate phase stability and chemical clustering.
Atomic diffusion dynamics mediate phase stability and chemical clustering.
Reduced diffusion limits the formation of local chemical clusters.
Reduced diffusion prevents phase segregation and thereby maintains nanoscale structural stability.
After identical annealing, the equiatomic high-entropy nanoalloy will show less grain growth than the lower-entropy baseline.
After identical annealing, the equiatomic high-entropy nanoalloy will show less chemical ordering, phase separation, and clustering than the lower-entropy baseline.
The equiatomic high-entropy nanoalloy will have lower measured diffusion coefficients than the compositionally skewed baseline.
The lower-configurational-entropy baseline will consequently have faster diffusion and more pronounced microstructural evolution.
The prediction is limited to temperatures high enough to activate diffusion but below melting or severe oxidation.
Elemental interactions and composition can alter phase configuration and therefore may change the predicted behavior.
Similar or greater grain coarsening, clustering, or diffusion coefficients in the high-entropy alloy relative to the baseline would falsify the proposed mechanism.
